title: The Effects of Noise on Children at School: A Review
authors: Shield, B. M. and Dockrell, J. E., 2003
review_question: To review research on issues relating to the effects of noise on children at school, including factors affecting speech intelligibility, academic performance, annoyance, and classroom noise levels.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review covers research from the past 30 years, primarily focusing on primary school age children (5 to 11 years), and includes studies on chronic exposure to environmental noise and internal classroom noise.

findings.consequent: Learning and attainments of primary school children
findings.quote: It is generally accepted that noise has a detrimental effect upon the learning and attainments of primary school children
both of which concluded that chronic noise exposure of young children has a particularly detrimental effect upon their reading ability.
the general effects of chronic noise exposure on children are deficits in sustained attention and visual attention
poorer auditory discrimination and speech perception

findings.consequent: Memory for tasks requiring high processing demands of semantic material
findings.quote: poorer memory for tasks that require high processing demands of semantic material

findings.consequent: Reading ability and school performance on national standardised tests
findings.quote: poorer reading ability and school performance on national standardised tests.
A major effect of noise and poor acoustics in the classroom is the reduction of speech intelligibility.

findings.consequent: Susceptibility to poor acoustic conditions (noise and reverberation)
findings.quote: young children are far more susceptible to poor acoustic conditions than adults.

findings.consequent: Detrimental effect of noise and reverberation on speech understanding
findings.quote: Children and adults who are hearing impaired are more seriously affected by noise and reverberation than those with normal hearing.
noise is the more critical factor and that criteria for acoustical conditions in the classroom should be based upon speech intelligibility.
the most important parameter for speech intelligibility is the signal (that is, speech) to noise ratio.
it is usual to assume that speech intelligibility will increase as reverberation time decreases to zero

findings.consequent: Impaired performance, poor long term memory, reading comprehension, decreased motivation (children 8-12)
findings.quote: high noise exposure was associated with poor long term memory and reading comprehension, and decreased motivation in school children.

findings.antecedent: Reduction in aircraft noise inside school (16 dB(A))
findings.quote: reducing the noise inside a school by 16 dB(A) had little effect on children's performance.

findings.antecedent: Removal of chronic aircraft noise source (airport closure)
findings.quote: even when the noise source is removed... it takes several years for the detrimental effects of noise exposure to cease.

findings.antecedent: Train noise (elevated railway, up to 89 dB(A))
findings.quote: children on the quieter side of a school next to an elevated railway had reading scores higher than children on the side exposed to the train noise

findings.antecedent: Noise abatement program (train noise reduction 6-8 dB(A))
findings.quote: after which no difference was found between the reading scores on the two sides of the school
there was a greater incidence of complaints about noise at levels above 60 dB(A) LA10.
exposure to traffic noise had a detrimental effect upon children's reading ability.
noise has a detrimental effect on children's attention

findings.antecedent: Aircraft and road traffic noise (66 dB(A))
findings.quote: Aircraft and road traffic noise were found to affect long term recall whereas the noise from trains had no effect.

findings.consequent: Standardised assessment test (SATs) scores (children aged 7 and 11)
findings.quote: There were significant relationships between external noise levels and SATs scores, the relationships being stronger for the older children.
Hetu et al [3] found a significant drop in children's performance, particularly in learning to read, when the background noise level interfered with speech.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic treatment (reduced background noise and reverberation in classrooms)
findings.quote: Children performed better in word intelligibility tests in the acoustically treated rooms, the improvement being particularly marked when other pupils were talking in the classrooms.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic treatment (reduced noise in classrooms, 75 dB(A) initial level)
findings.consequent: Letter, number and word recognition (pre-school children)
findings.quote: Following acoustic treatment to reduce the noise the children's performance improved in letter, number and word recognition.

findings.antecedent: Annoyance due to noise (older children, 13 and 15)
findings.quote: there was a significant relationship between annoyance and the effect of noise on schoolwork

findings.antecedent: Internal background noise levels (LA90) in classrooms
findings.consequent: Standardised assessment test scores (English test, age 11)
findings.quote: The test which showed the strongest association with noise was the English test of the older (age 11) children
background speech in the classroom interferes with general processing of language.
children's talk in the classroom had a detrimental effect upon the verbal (reading) task
the addition of random environmental noise events improved performance on this task.
A non-verbal (speed of processing) task was detrimentally affected by both classroom talk and environmental noise individually

findings.antecedent: Combination of classroom talk AND environmental noise
findings.quote: the worst performance occurring in a combination of these two sounds.
Children at school have consistently been found to be annoyed by chronic aircraft noise exposure
The older children were more aware of the noise
the younger children found noise more annoying.

findings.antecedent: Intermittent loud noise events (trains, motorbikes, lorries, sirens)
findings.quote: it is intermittent loud noise events which cause most annoyance to children while at school.

synthesis_conclusions: Noise has a detrimental effect on children's performance at school, with older primary school children appearing to be most affected.
Children experience annoyance due to noise at school.
Classroom noise levels can be high, especially in untreated classrooms, often due to classroom activity.
The degradation of speech intelligibility is a primary cause of noise's detrimental effect.
The precise nature of noise effects on children's cognitive processes is not yet fully understood.
There is increasing awareness among professionals about the need for good acoustic conditions in classrooms, reflected in current standards.
evidence_gaps: Further work is needed to examine the reasons for the effects of noise on children's performance, particularly what aspects of their cognitive processing are affected by different types of irrelevant noise.
The precise nature of the effects of noise upon the cognitive processes of children is not yet fully understood.

moderators.effect: Younger children are more susceptible to poor acoustic conditions. Older children are more aware of noise, but younger children are more annoyed. Relationships between external noise and SATs scores are stronger for older children.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Differential effects on speech intelligibility, annoyance, and academic performance.

moderators.effect: Hearing impaired children are more seriously affected by noise and reverberation than those with normal hearing.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Increased detrimental effects on speech understanding.

moderators.effect: Chronic aircraft noise, train noise, and road traffic noise all show detrimental effects on academic performance. Intermittent loud noise events cause most annoyance. Random environmental noise events can sometimes improve verbal task performance, while classroom talk has a detrimental effect.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Varying impacts on different cognitive tasks and annoyance levels.

moderators.effect: Acoustic treatment reducing background noise and reverberation improves word intelligibility and recognition skills in children.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Positive impact on performance in treated vs. untreated classrooms.

moderators.effect: High correlation between a school's external noise level and the percentage of children having free school meals, suggesting that deprived children in noisy areas may experience additional negative effects.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Potential exacerbation of negative noise effects in socially deprived populations.

limitations: Many studies focused on single noise sources, while classroom exposure is often a combination.
Few studies considered the effects of irrelevant noise in the classroom itself.
Data on classroom noise levels are often limited in scope and difficult to interpret due to changes in instrumentation, measurement techniques, and parameters over time.
Many other factors influencing children's performance (e.g., ability, language, social deprivation) are often unreported and may interact with noise effects.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Effects of Noise on Children at School: A Review
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper reviews research on issues relating to the effects of noise on children at school. Areas covered include factors affecting speech intelligibility in the classroom; the effects of environmental and classroom noise on children's academic performance; children's annoyance due to noise; and surveys of classroom noise levels. Consistencies and discrepancies between the results of various studies are highlighted. The paper concludes by outlining some current acoustic standards for classrooms.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Noise acts as a distractor, diverting cognitive resources from primary tasks, thereby impairing learning and performance.
Noise acts as an environmental stressor, leading to physiological and psychological arousal that negatively impacts cognitive function and well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: Noise exposure leads to cognitive distraction and increased cognitive load, which impairs attentional resources and working memory, ultimately hindering learning and academic attainment.
